Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Vikram, fifty-three, spent years working as a civilian logistics coordinator in a Middle Eastern conflict zone before a final push through a valley turned a routine supply convoy into a collapse of ground and steel. A sudden explosion tore through the air, a deafening bang that seemed to erase the sky. The impact pinned him beneath a twisted metal panel, knees drawn up, hands braced against the cab floor, utterly unable to direct what happened next. Dust and the sharp, acrid scent of burnt rubber and crushed earth filled his lungs. When the shaking finally stopped, the silence felt heavier than the noise. He walked away, but the valley stayed with him. In the years that followed, his body never stopped bracing. He was perpetually on guard, shoulders tight, jaw clenched, cataloging exits and counting windows. Ordinary noises—a car door slamming, a dropped wrench in his garage, a refrigerator compressor kicking on—made him jump as though shrapnel were flying. When the memories surfaced, his body simply slid back into that pinned position. His knees would lock, his hands would curl into the air, and the old dust would fill his throat. The grief would arrive then, sudden and heavy, overwhelming him until he could not speak. At the same time, the stories would slip away from him, too extreme to be real, too far removed from his quiet life in Cincinnati to belong to him. The tension in his muscles became a second skin, a constant hum of readiness that never faded. He and Priya, his wife, had lived through the accumulating shifts. He took on every painting job he could find, mixing primers, rolling walls, sanding drywall until his fingers ached and the hours blurred. He stopped reading the news, flipping past headlines about foreign conflicts, unwilling to let the broadcasts pull him back. When his mind turned inward, it looped on the same question: why him? He paced his kitchen at night, tracing the same routes, replaying the mechanics of the blast. The world felt like a place that could fall apart without warning, and he knew he was no longer the man who could navigate it. The precision that had once defined him—the steady hand, the even coat, the ability to plan a room’s light—felt like a language he had forgotten. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore; the work was just noise, the house was just shelter, and the silence between them at dinner grew wider. His work as a painter became a daily confrontation with what he tried to outrun. The thinners and aerosol propellants carried a sharp, chemical bite that mirrored the valley’s burnt-dust stench, and on job sites, the crack of a staple gun or the backfire of a delivery truck sent his heart hammering against his ribs. He found himself stepping back from ladders, checking his phone for alerts, and leaving jobs early when a sudden noise echoed through an empty apartment. His wife noticed the way he flinched at ordinary household sounds, the way he started leaving the house before dawn to avoid the evening television broadcast drifting from the living room. The missed deadlines, the unreturned client calls, the distance that stretched between them—these were the quiet changes that settled over their days. What finally brought him to the clinic was not a single collapse, but a Tuesday afternoon when he stood in a half-primed hallway, roller in hand, and felt his knees buckle as a garbage truck backfired outside. He tried to take charge of the cut lines, but the sudden noise shattered his focus and left him paralyzed by a familiar, suffocating lack of control. The smell of wet latex and dust filled his throat, his body locked back into that impossible position, and the grief rose so high it drowned out his own voice. He set the roller down, walked out to his truck, and called the number he had saved weeks ago. He does not know if he will ever feel steady again, and what frightens him most is the certainty that his hands will never hold a brush with the same trust. Yet, beneath that fear, there is a quiet, stubborn hope that somewhere in this room, someone might help him remember how to breathe without bracing.
